<reason>Both sides were sharp, disciplined, and well-grounded, but CON (A) won more of the decisive exchanges. A's pandemic school-board counter (saturation local coverage coexisted with more tribal conflict) damaged PRO's shared-object depolarization mechanism and was never squarely answered. A's anticipatory-compliance point — capture needs no public unlock, just a reporter who knows who renews the desk, leaving "no trace to vote against" — defeated B's central "public unlock" safeguard, which B kept reasserting without addressing the mechanism. A answered both pressure questions directly and generated new decisive ground (a captured desk certifies innocence for the incumbent-voting half and crowds out nonprofit alternatives), which B never reclaimed. B's closing "contradiction" charge was clever, but A's closing dissolved it cleanly: the desk is trusted by the in-group and distrusted by the out-group, producing both harms through one mechanism. B's strongest standing argument — the status quo already maximizes both harms — kept the debate competitive, but B's firewall answers were shown to "route through the network they must police," and B's follow-through on A's answers was thinner than A's follow-through on B's.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 answer on "darkness vs. captured desk": a publicly funded desk that never prints the story certifies innocence and forecloses donor-funded alternatives — "their desk does not fill the vacuum, it occupies it." It directly answered B's hardest pressure question and reframed the capture comparison, and A's closing then sealed it by resolving B's trust/distrust contradiction via heterogeneous audiences.</best_rebuttal>
